newsitem.title: SINGAPORE: Giant new submarine cable to feed off Internet.
newsitem.headline: Giant new submarine cable to feed off Internet.

text.p: A new Asia-Mideast-Europe optic fibre submarine cable will meet booming demand for phone lines -- including the Internet and business needs like tele-conferencing, analysts said on Thursday.
The 38,000-km (23,600-mile) network stretching from the South Pacific to the North Atlantic across Asia and the Middle East, will cost the 90 companies building it US$1.3 billion.
But the cable network will be a money-spinner that brings down the costs of international phone calls, the analysts said.

They said demand for fast, top-quality telecommunications was growing so rapidly that the consortium building what will be the world's biggest undersea network should recover its investment by leasing capacity to other telephone operators around the globe.

Fuelled by rising demand from the global Internet computer network and the ever more sophisticated needs of multi-media communications like video-conferencing, the network could even be fully employed when it comes on line at the end of 1998.
"This cable will help reduce the cost of international calls for everyone," said David Riedel, Southeast Asian telecommunications analyst at Salomon Brothers in Bangkok.
Giant new submarine cable to feed off Internet
"It is very exciting. It will allow telephone companies to route their calls via the cheapest possible connection, avoiding high tariffs and helping to bring down charges everywhere."
"The operators of the new cable will make money by selling capacity on the network to other companies," he added.
Ninety telecommunications groups from four continents signed an agreement on Wednesday to build the new cable, which will be the world's longest and largest-capacity submarine network.
It will serve three billion people when completed -- more than half the world's population -- according to Lee Hsien Yang, the head of Singapore Telecom Ltd (SingTel).
With an initial capacity of 10 gigabits of data via each of its twin cables, the SEA-ME-WE 3 network will allow up to 120,000 simultaneous telephone calls via 39 landing points.
This is effectively four times the previous biggest undersea network in Asia, which has a total capacity of five gigabits, a spokesman for one of the consortium members told Reuters.

The capacity of the new network may be boosted to 40 gigabits with a further investment of US$70-80 million, a move being considered by the consortium, said a spokesman for Japanese partner Kokusai Densin Denwa (KDD).
